text: An insurer receives 8,000 claims a day. Each claim needs the same intake steps: read the photos and adjuster notes, check coverage against fixed policy rules, and pay claims under $5,000 automatically. About 2% of claims are flagged for possible fraud, and investigating them is open-ended: the next step depends on what was just found. Which architecture fits best?
options: A single agent per claim with intake, coverage, and payout tools, and a PreToolUse hook that enforces the $5,000 limit
A code-driven workflow for every claim, with flagged claims passed through an extra fixed sequence of fraud-check prompts
A code-driven workflow for intake with limits enforced in code, and a read-only investigation agent for flagged claims
A coordinator agent that delegates photos, notes, coverage, and payment to parallel subagents for every claim
correct_answer: A code-driven workflow for intake with limits enforced in code, and a read-only investigation agent for flagged claims
explanation: Match the pattern to each part of the problem. Intake is a fixed sequence, so a workflow with code-enforced limits handles it predictably, and only the open-ended fraud slice needs an agent, kept read-only with a human deciding (C). Option A enforces the limit correctly, but gives an agent's cost and variance to 8,000 identical intake flows a day. A fixed fraud checklist (B) cannot follow an investigation whose next step depends on what was found. Parallel subagents (D) multiply tokens for steps that depend on each other, such as payment depending on coverage.

text: A due-diligence assistant uses a coordinator that spawns six research subagents for every request. Token cost is about 7x a single-agent design. Evaluation shows the multi-agent design improves quality only on broad reports covering several companies, while 60% of requests are narrow questions about one company. What should the architect recommend?
options: Route single-company questions to one agent, and use the coordinator and subagents only for multi-company reports
Enable prompt caching on the shared instructions that the coordinator and all six subagents re-read on every single request
Run the six subagents on Haiku at low effort, and keep the coordinator on Sonnet for the final synthesis
Merge the six subagents into two broader subagents, and use that design for every request
correct_answer: Route single-company questions to one agent, and use the coordinator and subagents only for multi-company reports
explanation: Multi-agent designs need a reason such as parallel breadth, and the evaluation shows that reason only exists for broad reports. Routing narrow questions to a single agent (A) removes most of the 7x cost where it buys nothing. Caching (B) is worth doing but still runs six workers on every narrow question. Downsizing the workers (C) is an unevaluated quality change that keeps the unnecessary fan-out. Two broader subagents everywhere (D) still overspends on narrow questions and may weaken the broad reports.

text: In a research system, each subagent returns a long narrative of everything it read. The coordinator's context fills up, it drops sources, and the final report contains claims that cannot be traced to any source. What is the best design change?
options: Give each subagent the coordinator's full conversation history so its findings stay aligned with the goal
Move the coordinator to a model with a 1M-token context window so every narrative fits
Enable compaction on the coordinator so older subagent narratives are summarized automatically
Require each subagent to return compact claims, each with a source ID and quoted evidence
correct_answer: Require each subagent to return compact claims, each with a source ID and quoted evidence
explanation: Context isolation works only when workers return compact, structured results. A result contract of claims with source IDs and evidence (D) keeps the coordinator's context small and makes every claim traceable. Sharing the full history (A) bloats each worker's context and does not change what it returns. A larger window (B) delays the overflow and still dilutes attention. Compaction (C) summarizes the narratives, which is exactly where sources get dropped.

text: A support chat assistant costs $0.09 in tokens per conversation and resolves 40% of conversations; each escalation to a human costs $7. Proposal 1 moves to a smaller model, halving token cost, but on the evaluation set resolution drops to 37%. Proposal 2 improves retrieval, adding $0.03 per conversation and raising resolution to 48% on the same set. Which should the architect recommend?
options: Proposal 1, which halves the token cost of every conversation
Proposal 2, which lowers the total cost per resolved conversation
Both proposals together, which cut token cost and raise resolution
Proposal 1 now and Proposal 2 next quarter, to bank the token savings first
correct_answer: Proposal 2, which lowers the total cost per resolved conversation
explanation: Optimize the metric the business pays for. Per 100 conversations, today costs about $9 in tokens plus $420 in escalations. Proposal 2 (B) costs $12 plus $364. Proposal 1 (A) costs $4.50 plus $441, which is more than today, so combining them (C) or starting with Proposal 1 (D) brings back its resolution loss. Token savings are real but small next to escalation cost.

text: An account-reconciliation agent runs sessions of several hours. Account IDs and amounts first appear in tool results early in the session. Server-side compaction keeps the conversation within the context window, but after compaction the agent sometimes uses the wrong account ID or amount. What is the best fix?
options: Move the agent to a model with a 1M-token context window and turn compaction off
Keep exact IDs and amounts in a persistent facts block that compaction does not rewrite
Lower the compaction threshold so the conversation is summarized earlier and more often
Use context editing to clear old tool results from the conversation instead of compacting it
correct_answer: Keep exact IDs and amounts in a persistent facts block that compaction does not rewrite
explanation: Summaries can drop or blur exact values, so keep IDs, amounts, and dates in a persistent facts block that compaction cannot rewrite (B). A larger window (A) only delays the problem and dilutes attention over hours of tool output. Compacting more often (C) creates more chances to lose a value. Clearing old tool results (D) removes the very results where the IDs and amounts first appeared.

text: An internal compliance tool sends a 30,000-token static manual as a cached prefix, followed by a short question. The breakpoint is placed correctly and nothing in the prefix changes. Requests arrive about every 20 minutes, and `cache_read_input_tokens` is almost always 0. What is the best fix?
options: Add a second `cache_control` breakpoint at the end of the manual
Send a small keep-alive request every 4 minutes to keep the cache warm
Move the manual into the first user message so it is cached with the conversation
Change the cache lifetime from the 5-minute default to 1 hour
correct_answer: Change the cache lifetime from the 5-minute default to 1 hour
explanation: The default lifetime is 5 minutes, refreshed on each hit, so requests 20 minutes apart always find the cache expired. The 1-hour lifetime (D) is designed for gaps of 5 to 60 minutes. Another breakpoint (A) expires just as fast. Keep-alive requests (B) work, but they add traffic and cost to imitate a setting the platform already provides. Moving the manual (C) does not change how long the cache lives.

text: A team built a remote MCP server for CRM actions. Users authenticate with OAuth 2.1, and the server forwards each user's access token unchanged to the downstream CRM API. What should the security review flag?
options: Token passthrough: the server should call the CRM with its own scoped credentials
The server should use one shared CRM service account for all upstream calls
The tokens should be bound to the user's IP address to prevent replay
Nothing: forwarding the user's own token keeps their identity end to end
correct_answer: Token passthrough: the server should call the CRM with its own scoped credentials
explanation: MCP servers must not pass the client's token through to upstream APIs. They accept only tokens issued for them and call upstream with their own scoped credentials (A). A shared service account (B) creates a confused deputy with broad rights. IP binding (C) does not fix a token being used for an audience it was not issued for. Option D sounds safe, but passthrough skips audience validation and lets a token minted for one service be replayed against another.

text: A policy assistant serves 30 departments. Users report two problems: answers sometimes cite a superseded version of a policy, and occasionally an answer quotes another division's confidential guidelines. Retrieval uses hybrid search with a reranker. What is the most effective change?
options: Rerank a larger candidate set so that current policy versions rise to the top
Require every answer to cite the document version and show it to the user
Filter on document status and the user's department access before ranking
Rebuild the index with a blue/green refresh and a retrieval evaluation gate
correct_answer: Filter on document status and the user's department access before ranking
explanation: Both problems are about which chunks are allowed into the context. A metadata filter on status and access rights applied before ranking (C) keeps stale and unauthorized chunks out entirely. Reranking (A) still ranks old and confidential versions. Version citations (B) make the problem visible but do not prevent it. A blue/green rebuild (D) is a safe refresh practice, but without a status and access filter the same chunks are retrieved again.

text: A bank's onboarding agent must request background checks from an independent KYC vendor. The vendor runs its own agent, owns its own lifecycle and policies, and returns results hours later. Which integration fits best?
options: A2A task delegation to the vendor's agent
An MCP server that wraps the vendor's API as tools
A subagent in the bank's application that calls the vendor
A direct API call to the vendor, polled until results arrive
correct_answer: A2A task delegation to the vendor's agent
explanation: A2A is for delegating to an agent that another organization owns and operates, with discovery and a task lifecycle for long-running work (A). An MCP wrapper (B) exposes tools, not an independently operated agent with its own policies. A subagent (C) is in-process delegation inside one application. A polled API call (D) treats the vendor's agent as a plain endpoint and loses the task lifecycle that A2A defines.

Measured on that set: Opus at high effort scores 93% at 3.4 s; Sonnet at medium effort scores 91% at 1.6 s; Haiku at low effort scores 82% at 0.7 s. Which configuration should the architect choose?
options: Opus at high effort, with streaming enabled to cut time to first token
Sonnet at medium effort, with no other changes
Haiku at low effort, escalating low-confidence answers to Sonnet
Opus at medium effort, with prompt caching on the system prompt
correct_answer: Sonnet at medium effort, with no other changes
explanation: Choose the configuration that meets every agreed constraint on measured data: Sonnet at medium effort (B) is under 2 seconds and above the 90% floor. Opus at medium effort (D) has not been measured; a configuration decision needs evidence.

text: A claims-extraction system scores 97% on an evaluation set of 300 cases sampled at random from last month's traffic. About 90% of those cases are simple typed forms. Production complaints come mostly from handwritten and multi-page forms, which are rare. What should the team change first?
options: Double the random sample to 600 cases to narrow the margin of error
Switch from exact-match graders to a calibrated LLM judge
Add the 20 complaint cases to the regression set and keep the current sample
Stratify the set by form type and risk, and report scores per slice
correct_answer: Stratify the set by form type and risk, and report scores per slice
explanation: An evaluation set should cover cases in proportion to risk, not just volume, and report results per slice (D), so the weak form types become visible. A bigger random sample (A) keeps the same 90% mix. An LLM judge (B) changes how answers are graded, not which cases are tested. Adding past complaints to the regression set (C) is good practice, but 20 cases among 300 still leave the hard slices too small to measure.

text: One release changed three things at once: a new system prompt, a model alias that now resolves to a newer model, and a new retrieval configuration. Accuracy on the golden set dropped 8 points, and the drop is consistent across three runs. What is the most rigorous next step?
options: Pin the model ID back to the previous model, then re-run the golden set to confirm the fix
Tune the new prompt on the failing cases until the golden set recovers
From the known-good baseline, apply each change alone and re-run the golden set
Grade the failing answers with an LLM judge to see which part went wrong
correct_answer: From the known-good baseline, apply each change alone and re-run the golden set
explanation: Isolate the cause by changing one variable at a time against a known-good baseline (C). Pinning the model back (A) tests only one of three suspects, and the drop may come from retrieval. Tuning the prompt on the failing cases (B) can mask a retrieval or model problem and overfits to the set. A judge (D) describes the failures but cannot say which change caused them.

text: A nightly job extracts fields from 100,000 documents with Sonnet. Each request has the same 4,000-token instruction and schema prefix. Results are needed by morning, and the budget must shrink without risking quality. In what order should the levers be applied?
options: Switch the job to Haiku first, then add prompt caching and the Message Batches API
Add prompt caching and batching first, then test a smaller model on the eval set
Lower `max_tokens` on every request first, then add prompt caching to the prefix
Shorten the instruction prefix first, then move to the Message Batches API
correct_answer: Add prompt caching and batching first, then test a smaller model on the eval set
explanation: Caching and batching are free wins that do not change output quality, so they come first (B). A smaller model is a quality trade-off that must pass the evaluation set before it ships. Switching models first (A) takes the quality risk before the safe savings. Capping `max_tokens` (C) risks truncated output and saves little. Shortening the prefix (D) can remove instructions the extraction needs.

text: A European customer exercises the GDPR right to erasure. Their personal data appears in application logs, an evaluation dataset, a vector index, and an agent's memory files. Which design meets the requirement?
options: Delete the database record, and let log retention expire the remaining copies
Delete from the database and vector index, and pseudonymize the logs and eval sets
Delete the database record, and ask the model provider to delete conversation data
Delete by subject ID across the logs, eval datasets, vector index, and memory files
correct_answer: Delete by subject ID across the logs, eval datasets, vector index, and memory files
explanation: Personal data persists wherever the system stored it, so erasure must be designed as delete-by-subject or document ID across every store (D). Waiting for logs to age out (A) is a weak substitute for deletion. Pseudonymized data (B) is still personal data and leaves the memory files untouched. The provider request (C) misses where the data actually lives: the organization's own logs, datasets, indexes, and memory.

text: Adjusters review AI-extracted claim fields before payment. Reviewers now approve 99.6% of items in about 8 seconds each, and an audit found errors that reviewers approved. What is the best change to the review design?
options: Show source excerpts beside each field, flag contested values, and audit sampled approvals
Add a second reviewer so every claim gets two independent approvals
Raise the confidence threshold so fewer items reach reviewers, and auto-approve the rest
Track each reviewer's approval rate, and retrain those who approve too quickly
correct_answer: Show source excerpts beside each field, flag contested values, and audit sampled approvals
explanation: This is automation bias: reviewers rubber-stamp AI output. Putting source evidence beside each field, flagging contested values, and auditing sampled approvals (A) makes each review meaningful. A second reviewer (B) doubles the cost and can rubber-stamp the same way. Auto-approving more items (C) sends the errors that reviewers already miss straight to payment. Retraining reviewers (D) treats a design problem as a people problem.

text: Before launching a loan-support assistant, the team wants to know whether a customer's dialect changes how often the assistant escalates or refuses. Which test answers that question?
options: Review a random sample of 200 beta transcripts for signs of biased behavior
Track escalation and refusal rates by customer segment after launch
Run pairs of real cases that differ only in dialect, and compare the outcomes
Run a red-team suite of adversarial prompts written in several dialects
correct_answer: Run pairs of real cases that differ only in dialect, and compare the outcomes
explanation: Counterfactual testing changes one attribute, here dialect, and compares outcomes, so any difference is caused by that attribute alone (C). A random transcript review (A) cannot separate dialect from everything else that varies. Segment monitoring (B) is valuable, but it happens after launch and the question is about before launch. A red-team suite (D) tests resistance to attacks, not whether ordinary customers are treated differently.

text: A claims-summary assistant is ready for 400 adjusters. The sponsor wants it to finalize summaries without review from day one to show value quickly. Compliance is nervous. What rollout should the architect propose?
options: Shadow mode, then assisted mode, then autonomy for low-risk categories, each with exit criteria
Full autonomy for all adjusters, with a weekly stratified sample reviewed by compliance
A one-month pilot with 10 adjusters, then full autonomy for everyone if the pilot succeeds
Assisted mode for all adjusters, with a human approving every summary indefinitely
correct_answer: Shadow mode, then assisted mode, then autonomy for low-risk categories, each with exit criteria
explanation: A staged rollout (A) earns trust with evidence: shadow mode compares AI output with human work, assisted mode measures acceptance and edit rates, and autonomy expands only for low-risk categories that meet exit criteria agreed in advance. Weekly sampling (B) finds problems after they reach records. A small pilot (C) is a reasonable step, but it jumps straight to full autonomy for every category. Permanent assisted mode (D) ignores the sponsor's goal even where risk is low.

text: An assistant has a quality SLO of 95% of sampled answers rated correct each week. By Wednesday the weekly error budget is already spent. A prompt change for a new feature is ready to release. What should happen?
options: Release the feature, which only adds a new intent to the prompt
Release the feature behind a flag to 5% of users while quality is investigated
Re-baseline the SLO at 93% using this month's measured quality
Pause releases until quality recovers, and work on the cause of the failures
correct_answer: Pause releases until quality recovers, and work on the cause of the failures
explanation: An error budget works like uptime: when it is spent, releases pause until quality recovers (D), and the team works on the cause. Releasing anyway (A) assumes a prompt change is isolated, which is exactly the risk the budget guards against. A 5% flag (B) is a good release practice in normal times, but it still adds change while the system is below target. Re-baselining (C) lowers the commitment instead of meeting it.

text: An architect is handing a RAG assistant to the client's operations team. Which evidence best shows that the team is ready to own it?
options: The architecture diagrams, ADRs, and runbooks are complete and signed off
The architect stays on call alongside the operations team for six months
The team has run each runbook in a drill, and every alert has an owner
The team has completed training and passed a knowledge check on the system
correct_answer: The team has run each runbook in a drill, and every alert has an owner
explanation: Readiness is shown by doing: the on-call team has run each runbook in a drill, and every alert has an owner and a documented first response (C). Complete documentation (A) is necessary but does not prove the team can use it. The architect staying on call (B) postpones the handoff. Training and a knowledge check (D) show understanding, not the ability to respond to an incident.

text: An automated Claude Code review runs on every pull request. It posts many style nitpicks and several false positives per PR, and developers have started ignoring all of its comments, including real bugs. What is the best fix?
options: Move the review to the largest model, and run it at max effort on every pull request
Report only defined categories, and pause noisy ones while the prompt is tuned
Lower the review's effort and limit it to ten comments per pull request
Require an explicit reply to every review comment before a pull request can merge
correct_answer: Report only defined categories, and pause noisy ones while the prompt is tuned
explanation: Developer trust depends on signal: report only explicit categories such as correctness and security, and pause high false-positive categories while tuning (B). A bigger model (A) does not define what is worth reporting. A comment cap (C) can cut real bugs and keep nitpicks. Forcing replies (D) adds toil and teaches developers to dismiss comments faster.
